t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we become familiar with forensic chemical expert examination. Aim: to acquaint students with forensic chemical examination, its specific features, the plan of chemical-toxicological investigation and the duties of expert chemists. The plan consists of two parts: the report of the forensic chemical investigation and the chemical-toxicological expert examination. In the DVSSM course package the session is titled "Writing and defending the expert report".

As a result of the session the student gains information about forensic chemical examination, the bureau and its staff, as well as knowledge of the investigation report and the chemical-toxicological expert examination. Necessary items: the destruction product, filter paper, a funnel, reagents, test tubes, visual materials, adhesive tape and paper. The session is held in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities.

This is the session map. The plan: the report of the forensic chemical investigation and the chemical-toxicological expert examination. The investigation plan is based on the referral, the case history, the forensic medical report, the appearance of the object and the preliminary results. In the preliminary examination, appearance, smell, colour and the pH of the medium are assessed. Poisons are grouped by the method of isolation: volatile poisons, those isolated with a polar solvent, and metals, which are determined in the mineralisate. Finally, the report is written in three parts.

The expert chemist's analysis may be directed or undirected. A directed, that is, incomplete analysis is carried out on the basis of a forensic medical or investigative instruction for one or several substances. A full, that is, undirected analysis is carried out on the basis of a decision of the Ministry of Health. In a full analysis the expert chemist must carry out testing for 67 poisonous and potent substances.

The forensic chemist carries out the examination on the basis of a decision of the investigative authorities and, when the examination is finished, must write a report. The chemist must have higher education in pharmacy and must improve their qualifications every 5 years. The expert has the right to study the case materials, to request additional materials and to take part in court and investigative hearings. These rights are equal to those of the forensic medical expert.

In conversation with the victim or the victim's relatives, the expert does not raise their voice and does not ask questions that offend their dignity. Honesty, truthfulness and fairness are required of the expert. Keeping the causes of an accident confidential is the expert's professional duty. An expert who discloses information is held administratively liable.

t: Physical evidence: the route of receipt
n: The decision on the examination, the record, an extract from the forensic medical report and an extract from the case history are sent to the laboratory. The physical evidence is sent through the institution and entered in the laboratory's registration log. After that it is handed to the expert chemist and the investigation plan is drawn up. If the packaging has been broken, a report is drawn up first and then the investigation is carried out.

The decision on conducting the examination must necessarily state the commission of the crime, the physical evidence and the forensic chemist. If the decision does not state which poisonous substances to test for, testing is done for the substances approved by the Ministry of Health. An examination may also be carried out on the basis of a written instruction in order to give urgent medical aid to a poisoned person. If the packaging has been broken, a report is drawn up first, then the investigation is carried out.

There are three main logs in the laboratory: the registration log, the expert's workbook and the book of reports. The registration log consists of 16 sections. Daily records and calculations are kept in the expert's workbook. The book of reports is handwritten and, like the workbook, is numbered, laced with cord and sealed.

Storage periods. If the object has been preserved, it is stored for up to 1 year. Documents are stored in a safe and are discarded after 1 year. Objects containing alcohol are discarded after 1 month. When the amount of ethyl alcohol is determined, the report is printed in 2 copies: one for the organisation, the other for the archive of forensic medical examination.

According to the lecture, the report of a forensic chemical investigation consists of 4 parts: introduction, external appearance of the physical evidence, chemical examination and conclusion. In the section on external appearance, the packaging, container, seal, inscriptions, colour, smell, weight and pH of the medium are recorded. The chemical examination is the main part of the report. In it, writing chemical formulae or citing the name of an author is prohibited. The conclusion states the substances found and those with a negative result.

In the lecture, the report of a forensic chemical investigation is defined as consisting of 4 parts. In the laboratory session, however, the approximate structure of the act is three-part: introduction, description and conclusion. The description gives the appearance and the chemical examination, and the conclusion carries the signature and the time. In the conclusion, the substances found are recorded first, then the substances with a negative result. In the table, page 16 is given for the report and page 221 for the act.

Several factors must be taken into account when assessing results. A substance may be eliminated from the body before death occurs or may undergo metabolic changes. A substance may decompose completely or combine with other substances. If the sensitivity of the detection method is low, the substance cannot be detected. Therefore a substance not found does not mean that it is absent.

When a substance has been detected, quantitative analysis is absolutely necessary, because sometimes reactions characteristic of a harmless substance may appear. Such cases are as follows: the victim took the substance as a medicine, or the substance detected is naturally present in the object, for example metals. In addition, as a result of putrefaction of the object, reacting compounds may form, or a substance may be introduced from the external environment.

For the preliminary examination, microdiffusion, microcrystalloscopic reactions and chromatographic screening are mainly used. In referrals, examination of porcelain-like fragments with signs of white arsenic, that is, for Hg and As, is indicated by the Reinsch method. For arsenic, the Gutzeit method is applied. Methods of testing for hydrocyanic acid and nitrites are also used.

Poisons are grouped by the method of isolation. Volatile poisons are isolated by steam distillation: cyanide, acetic acid, halogen compounds, alcohol, aldehydes and phenols. Barbiturates, alkaloids and nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds are isolated with acidified water or alcohol. Heavy metals and arsenic are isolated by mineralisation. Dialysis, infusion with an organic solvent and special methods are also used, that is, for TEL, zinc phosphide and fluorides.

t: Methods of isolation: distillation and mineralisation
n: We compare the methods of isolation. By steam distillation, hydrocyanic acid, alcohols, formaldehyde, hexachlorane and nicotine are distilled. In vacuum distillation, substances are distilled at low pressure and at low temperature; this is convenient for substances that decompose at high temperature, for example TEL. Metallic poisons are isolated by wet or dry mineralisation, that is, destruction.

t: Methods of purifying the isolated substance
n: There are methods of purifying the isolated substance. Saponification is used for compounds resistant to hydrolysis, for example in purifying organochlorine compounds from fat. Re-extraction is based on changing the solubility of a substance by changing the pH of the medium. Sulphonation is for substances resistant to sulphuric acid, such as barbiturates. Fats and waxy substances are precipitated in acetone by cooling to −70 °C. Thin-layer and gas-liquid chromatography are also used in purification.

t: What the investigation plan is based on
n: Physical evidence is in many cases an irreplaceable object. Therefore the investigation is carried out carefully and economically. The forensic chemist first draws up a clear plan; the plan is based on a full study of the referrals and the causes of death. The plan takes into account the case history of the deceased and the report of the forensic medical examination. The appearance of the object, that is, pH, smell and colour, foreign substances and the results of the preliminary screening examination are also studied.

The number of poisonous substances is very large, and testing for each substance would take a great deal of time. The preliminary examination often makes it possible to exclude or suggest many poisonous substances in the plan. Remember: no conclusion can be drawn on the basis of the preliminary examination. If the screening result is positive, the main examination is mandatory. Some screening methods, although sensitive, are not specific.

t: Appearance, smell and colour of the object
n: If a foreign inclusion is visible to the eye or under the microscope, it is separated with forceps and tested for the suspected substance. Smell and colour give the forensic chemist a lead. The smell of bitter almonds suggests cyanides. A yellow colour suggests picric acid, strychnine, chromates or HNO3. A black colour indicates sulphuric acid, and porcelain-like crystals may indicate arsenic oxide. In a putrefied object the smell of poisons changes.

The medium is determined with indicators: litmus 5.0–8.0, Congo red 3.0–5.2, phenolphthalein 8.2–10.0, and also universal indicator papers. If the pH is 3 or lower, mineral acids or large amounts of organic acids are mainly present. A weakly acidic medium in putrefied organs more often indicates a fermentation process. An alkaline medium gives a lead for testing the object for alkalis or carbonates.

t: Groups of poisons by method of isolation
n: Depending on the method of isolation, poisons are divided into groups; some of them can be isolated by several methods. By steam distillation, cyanide, acetic acid, alcohol and phenol are isolated. With acidified water or alcohol, barbiturates and alkaloids. By mineralisation, that is, ashing, heavy metals and arsenic. By dialysis or infusion with water, mineral acid, alkali and alkaline salt. Infusion with an organic solvent, that is, for pesticides, and special methods are also used.

Some substances are isolated by several methods. Chloral hydrate and phenol, besides steam distillation, are also isolated by acidified water and alcohol, an organic solvent, or infusion with water. Liquid alkaloids are isolated by acidified water and alcohol and by distillation. Chlorophos is isolated by steam distillation, acidified water and alcohol, and ether infusion. The results are compared, and the method by which the most substance was isolated is chosen.

We give examples of screening methods. For barbiturates, cobalt acetate is added to the urine under ammonia or lithium hydroxide conditions. For phenothiazine derivatives, if an iron chloride solution in sulphuric acid is added to the urine, a light red colour forms. In TLC "screening", the Radionov method separates 49 drug substances. The Kartashov method separates 83 nitrogen-containing poisons on the basis of 5 standard substances. Each of these methods can give a lead for the main examinations.

t: Sequence of analysing an unknown object
n: The sequence of analysing an unknown object is as follows. First the referral, the causes of death, the case history and the forensic medical report are studied. Then the investigation plan is drawn up. The preliminary examination is carried out by external appearance, pH, smell and colour. Poisons are divided into groups according to the method of isolation, and the necessary isolation method is chosen. Finally, after isolation and detection, the report is drawn up.

t: Rules for drawing up the report
n: Rules for drawing up the report. The report is written on one line of the notebook at a uniform interval, leaving no blank space, on both sides. The margin is left on the left of the first page and on the right of the second, so that stitching them together is easy. Blank lines left over are struck through.

t: What is prohibited in the report
n: Some things are prohibited in the report. Abbreviating words and sentences and putting conventional symbols are prohibited. Writing the name of an author next to reagents and writing the chemical formulae of substances are also prohibited. For some corrections, "corrected, to be believed" is written in the margin, and the forensic chemical expert must put their signature.

The report consists of three parts: introduction, description (descriptive part) and conclusion. The introduction and description are not given headings. At the end, the expert's signature and the time of writing of the report are indicated. That is, the structure is as follows: the introductory part, the description, the concluding part, then the signature and the time.

The introductory part records on the basis of what documents and by whom, that is, the student's full name, year and group, the investigation was carried out. The period and place of the investigation, that is, the name of the laboratory, are indicated. The physical evidence and the purpose of its examination are recorded. The full name of the deceased, the causes of death and a brief summary of the incident are given.

In the description, the external appearance of the biological object is characterised. The serial number, pH of the medium, consistency, whether it was preserved, and other features are recorded. This part is given without any heading, as a descriptive part.

In the chemical examination section of the description, the technique of isolating poisons from the biological object is recorded in detail. The methods of determining the quality and quantity of the isolated substances are also recorded. The analysis is written exactly as it was carried out, without abbreviating words.

In the concluding part, the poisonous substances detected are first indicated by name. Then the poisonous substances not detected are recorded by name. The conclusion is based on the result of the expert examination. The report is confirmed by the expert's signature, and the time of writing is indicated.

Before examining the physical evidence, the expert chemist becomes familiar with the documents and draws up the investigation plan. If the document states the purpose, testing is done only for the substances indicated; or for an unknown substance according to the general scheme of forensic chemical analysis. Wherever possible, at least two methods based on different physical or chemical principles are used. To increase the reliability of the substance found, at least two determinations are carried out from each object.

t: Qualification: structure of the report and conclusion (draft)
n: Results are given in the form of an "expert conclusion" or a "report of forensic chemical investigation"; it consists of three parts: introductory, investigative and final. In the "description of the object", the packaging, the inscription on the container, morphological composition, weight, colour, smell, reaction to litmus and preservation are fully characterised. In the chemical examination, the amount of object used is stated for each operation. In the conclusion, the substances found are recorded first, with their amounts, then those not found, then the answers to the questions.

Case 14. Urine has been delivered to the forensic chemical examination as the biological object; the colour of the urine is red. Task: to carry out the analysis and draw up a report. In the table, the columns type of problem, causes and way of solving are filled in: what is analysed, what is determined and what is recorded.

Self-check list for the report. Rules of writing: uniform interval, no blank space, both sides, margins alternating, blank lines struck through. Prohibitions: no abbreviations, conventional symbols, names of authors or formulae; corrections carry "corrected, to be believed" and a signature. Content: introduction and description without headings; in the conclusion, substances found and not found by name; signature and time are placed.

We conclude. The plan of chemical-toxicological investigation is based on the referral, the case history, the forensic medical report, the appearance of the object and the preliminary result. Poisons are grouped by method of isolation: volatile ones are isolated by steam distillation, metals by mineralisation. The report consists of three parts and is confirmed by the expert's signature.
